prompt: In simple exponential smoothing with alpha 0.5, what weight does the week before last get? Answer as a decimal.
Simple exponential smoothing with alpha equal to 1 is the same as which forecast?

choices.text: The mean of the whole history
choices.why: That is where alpha close to 0 leads.

choices.text: The naive forecast
choices.why: Right. All the weight is on the last week.

choices.text: A seven-day moving average of the most recent days
choices.why: A moving average weighs a window equally; smoothing never does.

choices.text: The seasonal naive forecast, which repeats the same week of last year
choices.why: Simple smoothing knows nothing of seasons.

prompt: statsmodels' simple smoothing forecast 8,893 orders for every week of 2025. Why the same number every week?

choices.text: The model only has a level, and the forecast of any future week is the level now
choices.why: Right. No trend and no season means nothing to make the weeks differ.

choices.text: alpha was chosen badly
choices.why: Any alpha gives a flat forecast; it only changes the height.

choices.text: A bug in forecast(1)
choices.why: It asked for one week because every week would have been the same.

choices.text: 2025 had no seasons
choices.why: 2025 had the same seasons; the model cannot represent them.

prompt: After the last week of 2024, a Christmas week of 7,743 orders, the level is 8,033 with alpha 0.9 and 9,171 with alpha 0.1. Which forecast for the first normal week of 2025 should worry you more?

choices.text: The one with 0.1, because it ignores the latest data
choices.why: It does not ignore it; it weighs it like one week among many, which is right for a holiday week.

choices.text: Neither; both are levels
choices.why: They differ by over a thousand orders, and one was dragged down by Christmas.

choices.text: Both equally, since smoothing cannot handle holidays at any alpha
choices.why: Neither handles them, but a long memory is barely moved by one.

choices.text: The one with 0.9
choices.why: Right. A short memory has just learnt a holiday as if it were the new level.

prompt: Holt-Winters fitted gamma = 0.000 on Panela's weeks. What does that mean?

choices.text: There is no season
choices.why: The season is there and is used in every forecast; it just does not change.

choices.text: The fit failed and fell back to a default
choices.why: Zero is a legitimate optimum: the season was stable.

choices.text: The seasonal indices were estimated once and never updated
choices.why: Right. Zero weight on new data means the season stays as first estimated.

choices.text: The season is additive after all, so the multiplicative indices were switched off
choices.why: gamma is a memory, not a switch between model types.

prompt: Holt-Winters forecast 7,669 orders for the week ending 16 February 2025, and 8,767 happened. By how many orders was it too low?

choices.text: Orders were rising faster than the trend expected
choices.why: The neighbouring weeks were forecast well; one week alone was off.

choices.text: Its seasonal index remembers Carnival in that week of 2024

choices.text: February is always a quiet month in Brazil, and the model learnt that
choices.why: That would lower every February week, not one.

choices.text: alpha was too small
choices.why: The level was fine for the weeks around it.

prompt: What does seasonal_order=(0, 1, 0, 52) do to weekly data?

choices.text: Subtracts the same week of last year from each week
choices.why: Right. One seasonal difference.

choices.text: Adds a 52-week moving average
choices.why: The MA in ARIMA is about errors, and the 0 says there is none here.

choices.text: Fits one autoregressive term per week of the year, 52 in total
choices.why: The seasonal AR order is the first number, and it is 0.

choices.text: Removes the last 52 weeks
choices.why: Differencing loses the first season, not the last, and it transforms rather than removes.

prompt: A colleague says the MA term of their ARIMA model is a moving average of the last weeks' orders. What is wrong?

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: The name misleads exactly this way.

choices.text: It is a moving average of the last weeks' forecasts
choices.why: Close, but it is the errors, not the forecasts.

choices.text: MA is the differencing step, the I in the name
choices.why: Differencing is the I.

choices.text: The MA term uses past forecast errors, not past values
choices.why: Right. Past values are the AR term's.

prompt: Why does ARIMA difference a growing series before modelling it?

choices.text: Differencing removes holidays
choices.why: A seasonal difference brings last year's holiday along, as the Carnival forecast shows.

choices.text: To make the numbers smaller
choices.why: Size is not the issue; changing behaviour is.

choices.text: Its two other terms assume behaviour that does not change over time
choices.why: Right. Its differences can be stationary when its level is not.

choices.text: It is optional and only speeds the fit up
choices.why: Without it the model describes a series the data is not.

prompt: Which of these are pieces Prophet fits? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: A trend that bends at changepoints
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Holidays from a list of dates
choices.why: Right, which is how it handles one that moves.

choices.text: Autoregressive terms on the last weeks
choices.why: That is ARIMA's idea, not Prophet's.

choices.text: Smooth yearly and weekly seasons
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Which of Prophet's pieces would have stopped the February forecast error of this lesson?

choices.text: Changepoints, because the series bent
choices.why: The trend was fine; the problem was one week of the season.

choices.text: The holiday list
choices.why: Right. Carnival gets its own effect on its own dates, wherever they fall.

choices.text: A weekly season
choices.why: The data is already weekly; the error was in the yearly pattern.

choices.text: Extra regressors such as a marketing budget
choices.why: Nothing about marketing explains a holiday that moved.

prompt: An ARIMA model a colleague spent a week tuning does worse than repeating the same week of last year, on weeks it never saw. What should happen?

choices.text: Use the ARIMA anyway, because it is the more sophisticated model
choices.why: Sophistication that loses to a free baseline is cost without accuracy.

choices.text: Average the two and report the average
choices.why: Averaging can help, but only if it beats the baseline too, which is the same test again.

choices.text: Tune the ARIMA on the test weeks until it wins
choices.why: Then the test weeks are training weeks, and nothing has been tested.

choices.text: Use the seasonal naive forecast
choices.why: Right. A method that cannot beat the baseline should not be used.

prompt: What have forecasting competitions over thousands of real series found again and again?

choices.text: ARIMA beats exponential smoothing
choices.why: No family wins in general.

choices.text: Prophet beats both classical families on business data
choices.why: The lesson says the opposite of a general winner, and Prophet's own documentation names where it is weak.

choices.text: Simple methods and averages of methods are hard to beat
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: More parameters always mean a better forecast
choices.why: More parameters can fit the past better and forecast worse.

prompt: A team has two years of daily orders, a weekly and a yearly season, and a dozen holidays that move every year. Which family suits it best to start with, after the baselines?

choices.text: ARIMA, because it has short-term momentum
choices.why: Nothing in the description is about momentum, and two seasons plus moving holidays is ARIMA's hardest case.

choices.text: A model with seasons and a holiday list, such as Prophet
choices.why: Right. Several seasons and many moving holidays is the case it was built for.

choices.text: Simple exponential smoothing
choices.why: It has no season at all.

choices.text: Holt-Winters with a 365-day season
choices.why: One fixed period cannot learn holidays that move.
